nodes.date_label: Rulers, Townsmen and Bazaars (1983) · Empire and Information (1996) · The Birth of the Modern World (2004)

nodes.label: Robert H Wiebe
nodes.date_label: Businessmen and Reform (1962) · The Search for Order (1967) · Self-Rule (1995)
nodes.description: Historian of American social organization and democracy. Northwestern’s archival biography identifies The Search for Order as an interpretation of the transition from local communities toward bureaucratic organization. Ashley Woodiwiss’s substantial reading of Self-Rule emphasizes tensions between participatory self-government, centralization and hierarchy, while retaining the racial and gender exclusions of earlier democracy. These are historically argued models, not inevitable stages.

edges.relationship: Working People (1980, with Terry Copp) synthesizes labour conflict and organization within Canadian political development.
edges.evidence_note: John Bullen’s1981 opening assessment supports this contribution; no sole authorship or claim to inaugurate labour history.

edges.relationship: Morton’s writing and remembrance interpret soldiers’ wartime experience within Canadian nation formation.
edges.evidence_note: His quoted2018 interpretation of Vimy and his family’s remembrance supplies an own-voice example; national coming-of-age remains his contested interpretive position.

edges.relationship: Linteau’s contextual synthesis rejects a homogeneous Quebec explained by ethnicity or traditionalism alone.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview quotations on complexity and multiple determinants; collaborative synthesis is credited to Durocher/Robert and, for volume2, Ricard.

edges.relationship: Studies of Montreal and Maisonneuve foreground urban development and the city’s formative place in Quebec history.
edges.evidence_note: Own quoted urban argument and economic discussion checked in2012 interview; placement identifies research practice rather than membership in a single school.

edges.relationship: Nora’s lieux de mémoire distinguish lived social memory from historical reconstruction and examine their materialized sites.
edges.evidence_note: Own1989 pp7–9; the opposition is his argument, not a universal analytical law.

edges.relationship: Nora historicizes the national framework of French memory and its weakening, connecting historiographical practice to changing collective identifications.
edges.evidence_note: Own1989 pp10–12 discussion of nation, memory and historiography; selected French case, not a general claim about national histories.

edges.relationship: Cohen’s move from workers and consumers to a powerful planner retains social history’s attention to class, gender, race and ethnicity.
edges.evidence_note: Own BackStory answer on research design explicitly identifies the continuity and change; no assertion that biography replaces social history.

edges.relationship: Saving America’s Cities investigates how public redevelopment and residents’ participation changed across postwar cities.
edges.evidence_note: Own BackStory discussion of pluralist and participatory democracy, federal resources and community negotiation; urban renewal is assessed with both costs and achievements.

edges.relationship: Mosse examines nationalism through symbols, respectable conduct and the production of insiders and outsiders.
edges.evidence_note: Aschheim2023 substantial reading26:50–30:00; his qualification of Mosse’s bourgeois account retained.

edges.relationship: Mosse’s history of masculinity treats the normative male body as a component of national belonging and exclusion.
edges.evidence_note: Aschheim’s explicit reading of Nationalism and Sexuality and Image of Man,26:50–30:00; this does not claim complete women’s history coverage.

edges.relationship: Fallen Soldiers investigates the political transformation of wartime death and commemoration.
edges.evidence_note: Aschheim26:50 identifies appropriation of the war experience by the militant right; not automatic causal passage from all war memorials to fascism.

edges.relationship: Bayly’s global comparison traces interacting forms of modernity while retaining local and regional research.
edges.evidence_note: Own late2006 interview pp190–193; he explicitly refuses exclusive identification as a global historian.

edges.relationship: Bayly challenges depictions of an omnipotent colonial state and argues that empire depended on Indian intermediaries and uneven cooperation.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview pp189–190; critical engagement with colonial/postcolonial historiography, not membership in a unified postcolonial school.

edges.relationship: Berlin’s slavery history emphasizes variation across time and region and agency exercised within coercive relations.
edges.evidence_note: Own1999 opening points2–4; negotiation does not imply equality between enslaved people and owners.

edges.relationship: Berlin frames slavery through Atlantic migration and cultural exchange linking Africa, Europe and the Americas.
edges.evidence_note: Own opening points1 and5; comparative/worldwide framing does not collapse distinct slave societies.

edges.relationship: Bailyn’s population research locates early America within connections among Europe,Africa and the Americas.
edges.evidence_note: Own1981/1982 address opening; continental North America not a self-contained unit and process differs from a static Atlantic culture.

edges.relationship: The Ideological Origins uses revolutionary pamphlets to reconstruct historically consequential fears about power and liberty.
edges.evidence_note: Joyce Chaplin, Emma Rothschild and Charles Maier’s2021 memorial, paragraphs on pamphlets and political ideas; substantive named mediation, not exhaustive ideological explanation.

edges.relationship: Darnton reads symbolic practices of eighteenth-century French life through a historically situated anthropological approach.
edges.evidence_note: Own2018 answer52 acknowledges Geertz’s seminar influence and calls Cat Massacre anthropological; selected indexed passage, not complete interview.

edges.relationship: Publishing and clandestine-book archives connect intellectual production to circulation and audiences in pre-revolutionary France.
edges.evidence_note: Carla Hesse’s1999 substantial account of the publishing archive and literary underground; circulation does not by itself prove every reader’s response.

edges.relationship: Self-Rule interprets American democracy through participatory institutions and the constraints of centralization and hierarchy.
edges.evidence_note: Ashley Woodiwiss1996 reading; earlier white-male democracy’s exclusions remain explicit rather than an idealized universal democracy.

edges.relationship: Wiebe connects changing work relations and social hierarchies to the possibilities of democratic self-government.
edges.evidence_note: Woodiwiss’s Self-Rule discussion of transformed work, voluntary groups and the modern class system; substantive social interpretation, not merely a department label.
